tldr: TurboVLA rethinks the design of placing a massive LLM at the core of robot control. Instead, it directly connects a lightweight BERT with visual features through bidirectional cross-attention. With just 0.2B parameters and 0.9 GB VRAM, it achieves 32 Hz real-time control while hitting a high 97.7% success rate on the LIBERO benchmark.
hero_caption: Comparison of deployment setups and inference speeds between conventional LLM-centric VLAs and TurboVLA. Conventional setups rely on running massive foundation models on cloud servers with roughly 93 ms latency (~11 Hz). In contrast, TurboVLA enables fast edge control on a single RTX 4090 with less than 1 GB VRAM at 31.2 ms (32 Hz).
overview:
Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models, which integrate vision, language, and actions, have gained huge attention as a powerful framework for robotic manipulation guided by natural language instructions. However, most existing methods place a multi-billion-parameter large language model (LLM) at their core. They follow an indirect $V \rightarrow L \rightarrow A$ pathway, projecting visual features into the LLM's token space before generating actions. While this setup yields strong generalization, it introduces large inference latency and heavy GPU memory consumption, creating a serious bottleneck for real-time robot control.

To tackle this, the authors asked a fundamental question: "Do we really need a multi-billion-parameter generative LLM for low-level action execution?" When a task instruction is straightforward, like "pick up the red bowl," the robot does not need free-form text generation or complex long-horizon planning. Instead, it simply needs to determine where to look in the current image based on the instruction. Based on this insight, the authors developed TurboVLA ($V + L \rightarrow A$), a new paradigm that removes the LLM to connect vision and language directly. It uses a lightweight text encoder (BERT) and a vision backbone (DINOv3), generating compact action representations directly through bidirectional cross-attention.

Experiments were conducted across the standard LIBERO benchmark, the bimanual RoboTwin 2.0 benchmark, and a real-world robot arm (AgileX Piper). Despite having only 0.2B parameters and consuming just 0.9 GB VRAM, TurboVLA achieved a 97.7% success rate on LIBERO, matching or outperforming prior approaches based on 3B+ parameter LLMs (such as $\pi_{0.5}$). Its inference latency is also extremely low at 31.2 ms (32 Hz), clearly showing that practical, real-time control is fully possible with minimal compute resources.
contributions: Re-examined the necessity of the LLM-centric ($V \rightarrow L \rightarrow A$) pathway for low-level control, proposing TurboVLA as an LLM-free, direct $V + L \rightarrow A$ paradigm.

Designed an extremely simple and efficient architecture that directly exchanges information between a lightweight text encoder and visual features via bidirectional cross-attention to output ACT-style continuous action chunks.
Achieved a 0.2B parameter count, less than 0.9 GB VRAM consumption, and 31.2 ms inference latency (32 Hz control) on a consumer-grade RTX 4090, while setting a top-tier 97.7% success rate on LIBERO.
Demonstrated practical manipulation capabilities that rival or outperform prior models several times larger, spanning simulators, bimanual manipulation (RoboTwin 2.0), and a real-world robot arm.

sections.heading: Why put a massive LLM in the middle of robot control?
sections.summary: Conventional VLA models rely on LLM-centric architectures, leading to high latency and heavy memory usage. Recognizing that language generation is unnecessary for low-level control, this work proposes TurboVLA, directly connecting vision and a lightweight text encoder.
sections.details:
VLA models that unify vision, natural language instructions, and robot actions into a single model have developed rapidly. However, existing models such as RT-2 and OpenVLA rely on a $V \rightarrow L \rightarrow A$ pathway centered around multi-billion-parameter LLMs. In these methods, visual features are projected into the LLM token space, which imposes substantial computational cost and memory overhead at each inference step. This has been a major barrier to real-time, high-frequency control.

Recent studies have explored attaching action experts that output continuous actions instead of predicting action tokens autoregressively one by one. Even so, these methods still route everything through an LLM backbone, leaving the underlying computational bottleneck unresolved.

Here, the authors raise an essential question: "Do we really need a general-purpose generative LLM just to execute instructed actions?" When given a concrete task instruction, a low-level policy only needs to use the referenced objects and spatial relations to decide where and how to move in the image, rather than generating free-form text or conducting high-level reasoning. In other words, a lightweight text encoder like BERT combined with direct interaction inspired by vision-language grounding should be more than enough.

This insight led to TurboVLA. It independently encodes vision and language, binds them directly through lightweight bidirectional cross-attention, and predicts action chunks. As a result, it achieves 31.2 ms (32 Hz) high-speed inference on a single RTX 4090, requires less than 1 GB VRAM, and reaches a top-tier 97.7% task success rate all at once.

By enabling direct interaction without an LLM, TurboVLA slashes model size by up to 41x while delivering outstanding success rates and drastically lower latency.

sections.heading: Lineage of prior work: foundation models and efficiency efforts
sections.summary: This section reviews the evolution of VLA models and past attempts to make them efficient. While most prior works focus on superficial optimizations around giant multimodal models, this work takes a radical step by removing the LLM from the execution path entirely.
sections.details:
Related work can be organized into three main lines:

- **Evolution of Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models**: Adapting pre-trained large models for action prediction has been the dominant trend, as seen in RT-1, RT-2, and OpenVLA. The field has evolved rapidly toward richer representations, introducing continuous control heads like $\pi_0$ and $\pi_{0.5}$, incorporating diffusion models, or integrating world models and latent reasoning. However, all of these still rely on massive generative backbones.

- **Efficiency approaches for VLA models**: Researchers have explored various acceleration techniques, such as action chunking to avoid serial token generation, model quantization, token pruning/reduction, distillation, and asynchronous execution. Lightweight VLAs like TinyVLA and SmolVLA have also emerged. Yet, they remain confined to the paradigm of shrinking a pre-trained multimodal LLM.

- **Language interfaces in robot control**: Early works like CLIPort, BC-Z, and CALVIN treated language purely as task-conditioning features without routing through an LLM. TurboVLA revisits this idea within modern VLA frameworks, showing that a compact text encoder coupled with direct vision-language interaction can achieve highly accurate, real-time continuous control.

sections.heading: Preliminaries: LLM-centric pathways vs. direct vision-language interaction
sections.summary: We review the structural computational dependencies in existing LLM-centric VLAs using mathematical formulations. We then introduce direct interaction via cross-attention, a mechanism well-proven in models like Grounding DINO.
sections.details:
Existing LLM-centric VLAs extract visual observations $\mathcal{O}_n$ with an image encoder $E_v$, project them into the LLM embedding space using a projection layer $P_v$, concatenate them with instruction tokens $\operatorname{Tok}(x)$, and feed them into the LLM ($F_L$).

The key takeaway is that the LLM stage acts as the central interface connecting vision to action, rather than just a text processor. Whether using autoregressive generation or a continuous action head, the action decoder relies completely on the features $H_n^L$ produced by the LLM. This is the indirect $V \rightarrow L \rightarrow A$ structure.

In contrast, this paper focuses on direct, bidirectional vision-language interaction via cross-attention. Given visual features $Z^v$ and text features $Z^l$, setting one as the query and the other as key-value pairs allows computing language-conditioned visual features and vision-aware text features directly. Borrowing this proven mechanism from vision-language grounding (such as object detection), TurboVLA applies it directly to feature representation for robot action prediction.

sections.heading: TurboVLA architecture: direct connections and parallel predictions
sections.summary: TurboVLA consists of a lightweight text encoder, an image encoder, a bidirectional cross-attention interaction module, and an ACT-style action decoder. It bypasses LLMs entirely, predicting continuous action chunks in parallel.
sections.details:
TurboVLA's overall architecture is remarkably simple and lean.

### 4.1 Multimodal Feature Encoding
Task instructions $x$ are processed by a lightweight text encoder like BERT to yield a token feature sequence $Z^l \in \mathbb{R}^{N_l \times d}$. Instead of pooling them into a single vector, preserving the token sequence retains fine-grained details about target objects, attributes, and spatial relationships.
Camera images are converted into spatial features by a vision encoder (DINOv3). Positional embeddings and camera viewpoint embeddings are added before flattening into $Z^v \in \mathbb{R}^{N_v \times d}$.
Proprioceptive state information, such as the robot's joint angles, is kept separate from vision-language grounding and processed through a separate lightweight projection network $f_{\mathrm{state}}$.

### 4.2 Vision-Language Interaction Module
The independently encoded visual and text features pass through $N=6$ bidirectional cross-attention layers. First, instruction features are updated using image features (becoming vision-aware language features). Then, image features are updated using those language features (becoming instruction-conditioned visual features). This direct exchange constructs a compact, task-specific representation of what object to manipulate and how.

### 4.3 Continuous Action Chunk Prediction
The resulting multimodal representation is concatenated with the robot state features and fed into an ACT-style transformer decoder. Using learnable action queries $Q_a = [q_1, \dots, q_H]$, it predicts continuous actions across $H$ steps (an action chunk) in parallel in a single forward pass. Training is done purely via imitation learning (an $\ell_1$ loss on the action chunk), requiring no auxiliary language modeling losses.

sections.heading: Experimental results: unmatched speed, minimal memory, and high success rates
sections.summary: TurboVLA was evaluated across single-arm (LIBERO), bimanual (RoboTwin 2.0), and real-world robot (AgileX Piper) setups. It matched or exceeded the success rates of prior large VLAs while proving its real-time speed and low memory footprint.
sections.details:
### 5.1 Implementation and Evaluation Setup
The vision backbone uses DINOv3 and the language encoder uses BERT, with hidden dimension $d=256$ and $N=6$ interaction layers. Models were trained on 4 RTX 4090 GPUs using behavioral cloning ($\ell_1$ loss) with a learning rate of $5 \times 10^{-5}$ and batch size of 256.

### 5.2 Main Results (Simulation and Real Robot)
- **LIBERO (Single-arm manipulation)**: Across four suites (40 tasks in total), TurboVLA achieved an average success rate of **97.7%**. This surpassed the 96.9% of the 3.4B-parameter model $\pi_{0.5}$ (which has 93.6 ms latency). TurboVLA is about 17x smaller (0.2B), more than 3x faster at **31.2 ms (32 Hz)**, and consumes only **0.9 GB** inference VRAM. It also clearly outperformed recent lightweight VLAs like Evo-1 and VLA-Adapter in both speed and success rate.
- **RoboTwin 2.0 (50 bimanual coordination tasks)**: In the clean setting, it achieved an average success rate of **60.2%** with 43.4 ms latency, showing a clear lead over $\pi_{0.5}$ (57.0%, 95.6 ms) and StarVLA-$\alpha$ (50.3%, 74.9 ms).
- **Real-robot evaluation (AgileX Piper)**: Evaluated on four tasks—grab roller, move poker card, press stapler, and stack 3 bowls—TurboVLA outperformed $\pi_{0.5}$ on every single task (92.5%, 80.0%, 90.0%, and 87.5% success rates).

### 5.3 Key Findings from Ablation Studies
- **Necessity of language**: Completely removing language dropped the success rate from 97.7% to 70.8%, with goal-dependent tasks (LIBERO-Goal) collapsing to 11.6%. Natural language instructions also outperformed task ID embeddings (+2.3%).
- **Text encoder dependency**: Beyond BERT, using T5-small (97.1%) or SigLIP's text encoder (95.5%) yielded strong performance, showing robustness across language backbones.
- **Interaction design**: Bidirectional cross-attention (97.7%) performed substantially better than simple concatenation (95.2%) or unidirectional attention (96.1% / 96.5%).
- **Hyperparameters**: An interaction depth of $N=6$ and an action horizon of $H=12$ struck the best balance between performance and computational efficiency.

sections.heading: Conclusion and outlook: rethinking the role of LLMs in low-level control
sections.summary: TurboVLA clearly demonstrates that LLMs are not essential for low-level action execution. Future work points toward hierarchical systems combining high-level LLM reasoning with fast low-level executors like TurboVLA.
sections.details:
This paper proposed TurboVLA, moving away from conventional LLM-centric architectures toward a direct $V + L \rightarrow A$ mapping. By pairing lightweight encoders and bidirectional cross-attention with a continuous action decoder, it dramatically reduces model size, latency, and memory footprint while achieving state-of-the-art success rates.

These results urge the robotics community to reconsider whether general-purpose LLMs really need to serve as the central execution interface for low-level manipulation.

Of course, TurboVLA is designed specifically for executing low-level instructions. It is not intended to handle autonomous task decomposition or complex long-horizon semantic reasoning on its own. An exciting next step is building hierarchical architectures where an LLM handles high-level planning while TurboVLA executes agile, millisecond-level motor control.

takeaways: For executing concrete task instructions, a multi-billion-parameter LLM is unnecessary; a lightweight encoder like BERT with bidirectional cross-attention is more than enough.
Rather than simply concatenating tokens, bidirectional cross-attention that lets vision and language refine each other's context is exceptionally effective.
Keeping the model size at 0.2B and inference VRAM under 0.9 GB makes running 30+ Hz closed-loop control easy on consumer GPUs like the RTX 4090.
The findings highlight the promise of hierarchical setups: separating high-level language planning (an LLM strength) from high-frequency action execution (where dedicated models like TurboVLA shine).
limitations: Lacks the ability to perform high-level semantic reasoning or long-horizon task planning autonomously from abstract goals on its own.
Bimanual simulation experiments were limited by compute to training and evaluation solely on clean demonstration data without environment randomization.
Because it specializes in action execution, handling conversational ambiguity resolution or open-ended human feedback still requires a separate high-level planner.
